final:
In May of 1979, a Chicago commodities broker walked out his front door, told his wife he'd be back after a business meeting, and never returned. A court eventually declared him legally dead, and his family started collecting survivor benefits. But decades later, he was renewing a driver's license at a Nevada DMV, very much alive, under a name that wasn't his own.

Arthur Gerald Jones was forty years old when he left around noon on May 10, 1979, dressed in a tennis shirt and slacks rather than his normal corporate attire. He was frazzled enough that he left without his bracelet, the one he cherished. And before he sped away, as his wife Joanne recalled it, he said: "The meeting is not in a business office."

Not a reassurance. Not a destination. Just a location ruled out.

Before the exit, there was a life worth leaving — and Jones had spent years quietly dismantling it.

As a young man he worked delivery routes for his future father-in-law's store, Mr. Joseph's Liquor Cabinet, eventually rising to manage the place. From a liquor store stockroom to the floor of the Chicago Board of Trade is not a short distance, but Jones made it, becoming a commodities trader. The ranch house in suburban Chicago followed, sprawling enough to have a volleyball court out back. By any surface measure, the life had worked.

The gambling was eating it from the inside. Joanne told investigators he once put $30,000 on a single basketball game — not a season, not a run of bad months, one game. Desperate for cash, Jones forged Joanne's name on a second mortgage application. Then, a few months before May 10, 1979, he sold his Board of Trade seat outright to cover $210,000 in debts. The seat was the credential, the access, the identity — and he liquidated it.

He kept commuting to Chicago afterward. Joanne told investigators she didn't know for whom. She suspected the mob. Then in April 1979, a fellow commodities trader was shot and killed in his suburban home by masked intruders. Court papers would later describe Jones as having left shortly after that shooting to get a fresh start. The exit on May 10 was the last step in a process that had been running for years.

Investigators later found his abandoned silver Buick and a pair of sunglasses near O'Hare International Airport. By his own account in court records, he had paid an associate eight hundred dollars for a new identity.

For that single eight-hundred-dollar payment, he said, he received three documents: a fake Illinois driver's license, a fake birth certificate, and a Social Security card carrying a number that belonged to a real man. Not three separate transactions, not three separate risks — one exchange, one price, one complete kit.

Against the $210,000 in debts he had just sold his Board of Trade seat to cover, $800 was not a strain — it was a rounding error. What it purchased was something no amount of cash could build from scratch: a documented past. The driver's license said the state of Illinois had verified him. The Social Security card gave him a number the federal government already recognized as belonging to a living person. Each document authenticated the others in a loop that required no further explanation.

From Chicago he skipped around the country, stopping in California and Florida, before eventually settling. The criminal complaint described his stated reasons plainly: he was fleeing the mob and starting a new life. Whatever the proportion of those two motives, the $800 purchase had made both possible. Arthur Jones had not simply run. He had acquired a replacement, document by document, for the identity he was discarding — and then he used it.

Joanne was left with three children, and in 1986 a court declared Arthur Jones legally dead. Social Security issued $47,000 in survivor benefits to Jones's family — money routed to a widow and children who had no reason to question it, because as far as any court had determined, the man was gone.

That payment is where the story quietly doubles back on itself. The disappearance Jones staged to escape his debts had, within seven years, converted into a government check. His absence was the proof. The court's declaration was the mechanism. And Joanne and the children, who were the ones actually abandoned, became the conduit through which the fraud paid out — not to them as victims seeking justice, but to them as beneficiaries of a legal process that Jones had set in motion simply by vanishing well enough and long enough.

Las Vegas in the 1980s was where Joseph Richard Sandelli arrived and quietly took root. He and his longtime girlfriend settled into a neighborhood of stucco homes, dusty lots, and a scattering of horse corrals. They registered to vote. Not hiding, not invisible — registered, on a list, a civic participant. Arthur Jones had ceased to exist in any form the surrounding world could reach.

The girlfriend and her family knew him only as Sandelli. His attorney, Stephen Stein, put it plainly: "They had no idea about anything, which makes sense. Common sense tells you the guy's not going to go around telling anybody about this kind of thing." He had simply become someone else, and the people closest to him had no reason to look for a seam.

He found work that suited the name. According to his attorney, Jones worked at the Desert Inn, under a different man's Social Security number. That number belonged to a real person: an Arizona man named Clifton Goodenough. Jones had been using Goodenough's Social Security number in Nevada for years, and the record of that use had been accumulating under the Sandelli name.

Clifton Goodenough was a nurse at a Phoenix veterans hospital. Clifton Goodenough had never worked at a Las Vegas casino. But starting in 1995, his statements told a different story — year after year, they showed casino income earned in Las Vegas, income tied to a Social Security number that was his in name only. He fought the IRS for years over what he called "extra income" he supposedly had in Las Vegas. The agency garnisheed his wages. It pulled funds directly from his bank account. Every tax season brought the same fight, the same insistence that the income on the federal paperwork was not his. At some point, he reported the discrepancy to the Social Security Administration.

That report set off a chain with a very short fuse. Investigators traced the number to Nevada. Nevada's DMV records showed that a license had been issued in 1988 under the name Joseph Richard Sandelli, carrying Goodenough's Social Security number. And then investigators found something that made the whole thing concrete: in May 2008, the man holding that license had walked into a Henderson DMV office to renew it.

What Jones couldn't account for was that Clifton Goodenough was still out there — still filing taxes, still fighting a government that kept insisting he owed money on earnings he had never seen. That 2008 renewal was what led investigators to him. It was simply the moment when a live wire finally touched something it couldn't pass through.

Investigators reached Jones in July 2011, and when they asked him directly whether he was the Chicago commodities trader who had walked away 32 years earlier, he said yes. No elaborate cover story, no sustained denial. Just confirmation. Arthur Gerald Jones, who had been legally dead on an Illinois court's docket for decades, was standing in Nevada, alive, and he admitted it.

At the time of his arrest he was working the sport and race book at the Rampart, still under the Sandelli name. The Nevada state attorney general's office charged him with an array of fraud, identity theft, and related counts.

The plea deal that followed collapsed the charges into one. Jones pleaded guilty in September to a single felony — using a false name to obtain a driver's license or identity card — and avoided trial on the remaining charges, including identity theft, under the terms of the agreement with prosecutors. On January 31, 2012, Clark County District Judge James Bixler sentenced him. Jones was 73 years old.

The sentence was three years of probation. And then came the restitution, which is where the full shape of what he had done became visible as a dollar figure.

Judge Bixler ordered Jones to repay more than $78,600 to the Social Security Administration, the court's accounting of what the government had paid his family after the Illinois death declaration, with about $11,400 going separately to Goodenough, bringing the total restitution to $90,000. Now Jones would repay it. That $11,400 to Goodenough was for missed work and legal fees caused by the misuse of his Social Security number.

His attorney said the money would come out of Jones's own Social Security benefits.

That morning is where this ends, because it's where it started. A man walked out a front door, told his wife the meeting wasn't in a business office, and drove away. He promised to return. What he left behind: a wife, three children, and through the machinery of courts and federal programs, $47,000 in survivor benefits paid out in his name. What he built in place of that life eventually became a court order to pay it back. The door he walked through in 1979 was the same one the sentence closed behind him in 2012, just from the other side.
